newsitem.title: BELARUS: IMF letter sets terms for resuming Belarus credit.
newsitem.headline: IMF letter sets terms for resuming Belarus credit.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund has said in a letter to a senior Belarussian official that it would renew talks on a suspended credit to Minsk if the former Soviet republic undertook certain reforms by the end of March.

The Russian-language letter, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters on Wednesday, was written by the head of the IMF's European department and addressed to Prime Minister Sergei Ling. It said Belarus should adopt a new monetary policy of tying its rouble to the dollar or installing a floating rate.
The IMF froze a standby credit of $300 million in January 1996 over Belarus' slow pace of economic reform.
The letter said Belarus's monetary policy did not correspond to market demands and negatively influenced exports.

President Alexander Lukashenko maintains tight control over the economy by fixing prices, controlling the central bank and demanding the economy perform according to his economic plan, effective to 2000.

The IMF letter said Belarus central bank reserves fell to $9.5 million on February 1 from $47.5 million on January 1, dropping by $1 million daily due to energy payments paid to Russia's natural gas monopoly RAO Gazprom GAZP.RTS.
Belarus introduced a market rouble/dollar rate policy late last month to stimulate exports, replacing a fixed-rate regime of about 22,050 Belarussian roubles per dollar.
The rouble fell to 23,110 to the dollar on Wednesday from 23,030 to the dollar on Tuesday on the Minsk Interbank Currency Exchange.
The central bank sets a daily rate based on supply and demand on the exchange, adjusted for inflation.
One of the biggest concerns of international funding bodies has been the exchange rate policy in this country of 10 million people.
The IMF letter also spoke of the need for Minsk to stop rolling over enterprises' and organisations' credit repayment deadlines.
The World Bank said last month it would offer a $30 to $40 million loan to support small development and sign a loan memorandum soon if Belarus renewed an IMF macroeconomic reform programme.
Belarussian economic reforms have been running at a much slower pace than those in most other former Soviet republics.
